title: Bosveld Citrus grower system: first consultation

segments.text: Morning, everyone. Thank you for having me and thanks for the coffee, Johan. Um, before we start, there's one thing I need to check with all of you. I'd like to keep a transcript of this meeting so I can write up the requirements properly afterwards. And I use an AI assistant that runs on my own laptop to help me sort through the transcript.
Nothing goes to an outside service. Are you all comfortable with that?
Yeah, that's fine with me.
Yes, no problem.
Fine by me. As long as it doesn't end up on the internet somewhere.

It won't. It stays on this laptop and if anyone wants me to stop at any point, just say so. Okay. How was the road this morning by the way? I came in on the R seventy one from Polaquain and the stop and go at the pass was terrible.
Ag those road works. They've been there since Easter. My wife says they're building a new road one spade at a time.
It's worse in the

afternoon. The trucks. I'll leave early then. Okay, so I've read the email you sent, Johan, but I'd really like to hear it from you in your own words. Maybe start with the co-op itself, and then what made you pick up the phone?

Sure, so Barsfeld Citrus Cooperative, we're in Letzeidel, about 25 kilometers outside Tzanin. We pack citrus for our members, mostly oranges, valencias and navels, then some lemons, and a fair amount of soft citrus, the mandarins. The co-op was started in 1978 by 11 farmers.

And then. And today we've got, ah, about a hundred and forty member growers. Some of them are big commercial farms with a few hundred hectares and some are small growers from the nkawenkawa side with five or six hectares. Everybody's fruit comes through the one pack house here, behind this office.
and the pack house runs all year.

No, no. The season is roughly from the end of March with the early mandarins until about the middle of September when the last Valencias go through. Outside of that we do maintenance, we do the books and we argue about prices.
Mostly we argue about prices.

Yeah mostly. So what made me pick up the phone? Honestly it's the growers. They phone us all day. Where's my fruit? What was my pack out? When do I get paid? Why did my bins get downgraded? And we can't answer them quickly, because the information is in, I'd say, five different places.
And some of it is on paper.
Five different places. Can you walk me through them?
Precious can do that better than me. She lives in the pack house.
Yeah, okay. So it starts at the Weybridge. A

grower's truck comes in or a contractor's truck with bins on the back. Each bin is about 400 kilos when it's full. Okay. The truck goes over the waybridge and our clerk writes a delivery ticket. It's a carbon book three carps.

White carpi for the grower, pink for the office, yellow stays in the book. Handwritten. Handwritten. The Waybridge has a little computer with the scale program on it. It's called Waymate and it prints the weight on a slip. Then the clerk copies the weight onto the ticket, with the grower number, the
farm, the orchard block, the cultivar and the number of bins. So the weight comes from the machine, but everything else is written by hand. Exactly. Then the bins go into the holding

area. They get a a a cardboard tag tied on with the ticket number and they wait for the line. How long do they wait? It depends. In the peak sometimes two days. The early mandarins have to go through degreening first, in the rooms at the back, so it can be a while.

The oranges usually go the next day. Okay and then. Then the bins go onto the line. We've got an optical grader, the optosort, that photographs every fruit and sorts it into classes. Class 1 for export, class 2 for the local market and then juice.
The grader's computer makes a report for each batch. A batch is basically one delivery ticket. Right. And the report says how many cartons of each class and the percentages.
That's what we call the pack out. And the report lives on the grader's computer. It lives on the grader's computer. Tani Mariatji in the office
prints them out every afternoon and files them, and then she types the totals into a spreadsheet.
My spreadsheet? Well it's the co-op spreadsheet, but I built it.
Okay, so Saifo, the spreadsheet is yours. What does it do?

The spreadsheet is the heart of the whole thing, unfortunately. Every delivery is a row. Mariachi types in the ticket from the pink copy, and then she adds the pack out from the grader report. And then at the end of each month, I use that to work out the advance payments to the growers.
Advance payments meaning.

So in citrus, you don't get paid the full price when you deliver. The fruit gets exported, it goes on a ship, it gets sold in Rotterdam or wherever. And only months later do we know the final price. So we pay the growers an advance. So much per carton of class 1, so much per carton of class 2, a few rand per bin of juice.
MMHM. and then after the season there's a final pool payment when all the money is in.
Right, so the monthly calculation is the advance and the pool payment is once a year.
once a year, usually in February. And that one's a beast.
I can imagine. And the growers, how do they find out what they've been paid, and why?

They get a statement, I make it in the spreadsheet, and Mariachi prints it and posts it, or emails it to those who have email. Some of them still come and collect it at the office, they like to have a cup of tea with her.
How long after the month ends do they get it?
Um, honestly, three weeks, sometimes more, because everything has to be typed first and checked and then I have to reconcile with the bank.
And that's when the phone starts ringing.
So the growers are phoning because they don't know where they stand for three, four weeks.

Exactly, and look I understand them, a small grower with six hectares that's his whole income for the year. Yours He delivered thirty bins two weeks ago and he doesn't know whether they packed out at eighty percent or forty percent. Of course, he's going to phone.
How many calls
are we talking about? In the seism, I'd say, uh, Mariachi gets 40-50

calls a day, and I get the ones about the grading maybe 10 a day. Those are the angry ones. Why angry? Because when a batch packs out badly the grower thinks we made a mistake. He thinks his bins got mixed up with someone else's. And sometimes, to be honest, they did.
Because the cardboard tag fell off, or the ticket
number was written badly, and someone read a seven as a one. Okay, that's important. How often does that happen? Not often. Maybe, I don't know, two or three times a week in the
peak. But every time it happens it's a big fight and it takes a day to sort out. I have to go through the grader reports and the

tickets and phone the driver. Let me make sure I've got the picture. A truck comes in, it goes over the waybridge, the clerk writes a ticket by hand with the wait from way mate. The bins get a cardboard tag, they wait, they go through the optasort grader. The grader report gets printed, Mariagi types the ticket and the packout into Saifo's spreadsheet, and Saifo works out the advance at the end of the month and makes a statement.
That's it. That's the whole sad story.
In the fifth place, Johan said five.

Oh, the QC lab, sorry. Before a grower picks an orchard, our lab tests samples the sugar and the acid and the juice percentage to see if the fruit is mature enough for export. Maturity tests. That's on paper too, and the results go to the grower by WhatsApp.
Our QC lady takes a photo of the sheet and sends it.
Okay, and spray records. You mentioned export.

Yaw, that's a sixth place, now that you mention it. Every grower has to give us his spray records before we can pack his fruit for export, because the European buyers test for residues. Those are in a lever arch file in my office.
So there's paper and spreadsheets everywhere, and the growers can't see any of it themselves. That's really helpful. What's the most
painful part for you if you had to pick one?
The phone calls a no waiter The statements are because if the statements came out in a week half the
phone calls would go away.

For me it's the typing. Maraetchi types for what three four hours a day in the season, and she's retiring. When end of June next year, right in the middle of the season, which is a whole other problem.
That's a real risk, is there someone to take over from her?
Not yet. We'll advertise. But nobody else knows that spreadsheet like her and Saifo. She knows every grower by name. She knows whose son is farming now and whose wife does the books.
Okay, so let's talk about what you'd like. If this goes well, a year from now, what's different?

The growers can see their own deliveries and their pack out on their phones the same day or the day after. They get their statements in a few days, not three weeks, and we stop answering fifty phone calls a day.
Is there a number you'd want to hit? Fewer calls, faster statements.
Half, if the calls go down by half I'd be happy, and statements within, let's say, five working days after the month end.
Five working days is tight, but yeah, if I don't have to wait for the typing, it's possible.
Good. I'll write those down as the goals. Precious from the packhouse side. For me it's the tickets.
I want the way bridge to be quicker and I want the bins to be traceable without a cardboard tag that falls off in the rain. If every bin had a barcode or something
and you scanned it, then we'd always know whose fruit is on the line. Do the bins have anything on them today? A numbers. The bins belong to the growers mostly. Some have
numbers painted on, some don't. The co-op has about uh 3000 of its own bins that we lend out to the small
growers, and those have numbers burnt into the plastic. So putting a permanent label on each bin isn't straightforward. No, that's
why I said barcode or something. Maybe the barcode is on the tag not on the bin. A plastic tag that you clip on and it comes back to the weigh bridge. I don't know you're the expert.

I'm not sure I'm the expert on bins but I'll look into what other packhouses do. Let me note that as something to work out together. So scanning a tag at intake and again when the bin goes onto the line.
Yes, at the tipper where they tip the bins into the water. That's where we'd scan.
Hi sorry sorry. Is this the system meeting? Johan said half past nine I think. Or I heard half past nine.
It was nine Ryuan. Come in, sit. Ayesha, this is Ryuan. He does our IT. He's not staff, he's a contractor, but he's here every Wednesday and whenever something breaks.
Hi Ryuan, nice to meet you. We've just been through how a delivery goes from the weighbridge to the statement and Precious was talking about scanning bins at the tipper.
Odd okay, yaw the scanning, Precious has been on about the scanning for a year.
Because it's needed.
No,
I agree I agree.
Juan, it's actually a good moment for you. What's the network like? At the Weybridge and at the Tipper.
Uh so. The office and the pack house are on fiber. It came in two years ago and it's okay.
You know

But the Waybridge is at the gate, about three hundred meters from the office, and it's on a wireless link a point to point. When it rains hard, or when there's load shedding and the battery at the gate runs flat, it drops. The tipper is inside the pack house, so that's fine, the wi fi in there is decent.
How often does the weigh bridge drop?

in the season maybe once a week for an hour or so, and when the whole area's fiber goes down which happens, someone digs up a cable next to the R thirty six or whatever, then everything's off. Last year we had a full day once.
So the way bridge has to keep working without the network.
It has to. We cannot stop trucks at the gate. If a truck waits, the fruit sits in the sun and the next twenty trucks are behind it
on the road.
Okay, so the intake has to work offline and catch up when the link is back. I'll write that as a firm requirement.
Yaw, and to be honest, I can put a bigger battery on the gate, that's not expensive. But the fiber outages I can't fix.
Let's talk about Waymate for a second, is it something you can get data out of?

Waymate is old. It runs on a Windows PC under the counter at the gate. It writes every Waying to a little database file and it can export a CSV at the end of the day. MM. And I think the scale indicator is connected to the P C by a serial cable.
So if you wanted the wait live you could probably read it straight from the indicator, without weight mate at all.
That's useful, and the greater, the optosort.

That's the problem one. The Optosort was bought in 2019 from the supplier overseas through their agent in Cape Town. Its computer is locked down. The reports come out as PDFs. There might be a database underneath but we don't have the password and the agent says if we touch it, we void the support contract.
So getting the pack out out of the grater automatically is uncertain.
Very uncertain. I can ask the agent whether they have an export, a CSV or an API or something. They might want money for it.
Would you mind asking them, that's probably the biggest unknown we've got.
Loyal ask I'll send them an email this week.
Thank you. And if the answer is no, the fallback is someone typing the totals from the report, which is what Mariatji does now.
or reading the PDF automatically. Can't a computer read a PDF?
Sometimes, if the PDF has real text in it and the layout never changes, I'd need to see a few. Can someone send me some greater reports from last season? I'll send you some, good batches and bad
ones.
Perfect. And on the accounting
side, Saifo, what do you use?

We use Ledger 1 for the books. The payments to the growers go out through the bank in a batch file that I upload to the bank's Business Banking. The spreadsheet makes the batch file actually. Well, it makes a list and I copy it into the bank's template.
So the payment calculation is in your spreadsheet and Ledger 1 gets the totals.
The totals, ya, I journal them in at the end of the month.
Would you want the new system to calculate the advances or do you want to keep that in your spreadsheet for now?

Hem honestly, keep it in my spreadsheet for now. The rules change every season. The board decides different advance rates for different cultivars and sizes, and I don't want to phone a developer every time the board changes its mind. If the system gives me the deliveries and the pack out clean I'll do the sums.
I agree, let's not build the payment engine in the first round.

Okay, so that's a decision. The payment calculation stays in Syfo's spreadsheet for phase 1 and the new system gives him the deliveries and packout as an export he can open in the spreadsheet. And then the statement. Does the statement come from the new system or from the spreadsheet?

Umd, that's a good question. If the advance is worked out in my spreadsheet, the statement has to show the advance. So either I upload the amounts back into the system every month or the statement stays in the spreadsheet.
Let's leave that one open for now. I'll come back with a couple of options. It depends on how much work an upload would be for you each month.
Okay.
Can we talk about the growers' information for a bit? What do you hold about them?

names, ID numbers for the growers who farm as individuals, company registration numbers for the farms that are companies, VAT numbers, bank account details, physical addresses, phone numbers, email, and their delivery history, their pack outs and what they've been paid.
Okay, so for the small growers who farm in their own name, that's all personal information under Popia, and the bank details need care in any case. Who should be able to see what?

A grower must only see his own stuff. That's the number one thing. If grower can see what grower be got paid, I'll have a war on my hands. Right. Seriously, these people are neighbors. Their kids go to the same school, they sit next to each other in church.
I understand. So each grower sees only their own deliveries, hackouts, and statements, and in the office.

Me and Johan see everything. Mariachi sees everything except no, actually she sees everything too. Precious and the clerks need the deliveries and the grading, but not the bank details and not the money.

I don't want to see the money. So the roles are something like this. The office and management see everything. The packhouse staff see deliveries and grading but not bank details or payments. And growers see their own. Who changes a grower's bank details today?
Only me, and only with a letter
from the bank. Because there's fraud. And then Last year someone phoned, pretending to be one of our growers, and asked us to change his bank account. Luckily Maraechi knew his voice.
That's exactly the kind of thing to design for. So changing bank details stays a manual, checked process in the office and a grower can't change them from their phone.
Definitely not.
Good. And the weights. What if someone changes a weight or a bin count after the fact?
That must be recorded. Who changed it and why? Because that's where the fights are.
So an audit trail on every change to a delivery, who changed it, when, what it was before, and the reason.
Yes
and the grower should be able to see that it was changed, I think.
Hm maybe not the reason. Sometimes the reason is, you know, the driver counted wrong because he was in a hurry to get to the bottle store.
Okay maybe

not the reasons. I'll note that the grower sees that a delivery was corrected and whether they also see the reason is still to be decided. Juan, where would all this live? Do you have a preference for hosting?
Not on a server in the office, please. I don't want another thing to look after, and the power here isn't reliable. Some cloud thing is fine.
The board said the data must stay in South Africa. One of our members is a lawyer and he was very firm about that at the last meeting.
Okay, so hosting in a South African data center. That's a constraint, and it's possible with most of the big providers now.
Yaw, they've got Johannesburg and Cape Town regions.
Exactly. And for the waybridge, the tablet or PC at the gate would keep its own copy of the day's deliveries and send them up when the link is back.
And if the tablet gets stolen,
Good point. Then it should need a PIN or a login and it shouldn't hold more than it needs. The day's deliveries and the grower list, not bank details.
Okay, that works for me.
How long do you keep the records now? Tickets and statements.
The orderers say five years for anything financial. The tickets we keep are, I think also five years, in boxes in the storeroom. The mice eat some of them.
Five years then, for deliveries and statements, and when a grower leaves the co-op.
We keep his records for the five years, for tax, and then, honestly, nobody has ever thrown anything away.

That's common. I'll suggest that the system keeps a lever's records for five years and then flags them for deletion, and you decide. Let's talk about the growers themselves. How do they use their phones? What kind of phones?
Everything. The big farmers have iPhones and laptops, and their own farm managers. The small growers, a lot of them have cheap Android phones, and data
is expensive. Some of them, the older ones, their kids do the phone stuff for them.
So whatever the grower's use has to work on a cheap Android phone on a slow connection without eating their data.
Yeah, and I don't want them to have to download an app. Last time somebody made us an app, for the uh the study group nobody installed it. Twelve people out of a hundred and forty.
A web page they open from a link then, one they can save to the home screen like an app.
That's fine.
And SMS. Not everybody uses WhatsApp properly but everybody gets SMS. What would you send them?
When their batch is graded, your delivery number 4471 packed out at 78% class 1, something like that, with a link to
see the rest.
That's a nice one. Johan, are you happy with SMS?
SMS is fine. What's app costs money if you do it through the business, doesn't it Huan?
Ya it's per message through one of the providers. But SMS also costs about I think 25-30 cents a message.
Then let's say SMS for the grading notifications to start with and maybe WhatsApp later. Are you all okay with that?
You know Fine.
Good, that's decided. And how does a grower log in? Most of them won't want another password.
No passwords. They'll forget it and phone us.
One option is a code sent by SMS to the phone number you already have on file for them. They type the code and they are in.
if the number on file is right. Some of them change their numbers.
Then updating a phone number would go through the office, like the bank details, so nobody can take over someone else's account by changing the number.
Yeah, same rule.
Now language. The growers speak.
English Afrikaans Zitsonga Sepedi. Most of the small growers are Zitsonga speakers.
My mother would want Ir in Zitzonger, but she reads English too. Do you want the grower pages translated?
Hm, I don't know. It'd be nice. But the statements are in English now, and nobody complains. The statements
have to be in English for the auditors anyway.
So the minimum is English. Whether we also do Zitsonga and maybe Afrikaans for the grower pages, I'll leave open and I'll tell you what it would cost to add.
Yaw, let's see the cost first.
And how should it look? Do you have any preferences? Colors style.
Our colors are orange and dark green. The logo is an orange with a leaf on it. Use that. And big clear writing. Some of our members are 70, 75.
For the
Weybridge big buttons, the clerk sometimes has gloves on in winter and it's dusty, and it's outside under the roof but
outside, so the screen must be readable in the sun. Would that be a tablet at the Weybridge, or the P C? A tablet I think. A rugged
ones. The P C is under the counter and the clerk has to go inside the little office to use it while the driver waits.
Then it needs to be charged every day and with the battery at the gate.
We'll keep it
charged Ryuan.
Okay, okay.

I'll write it down as a strong preference for a rugged tablet at the Weybridge and I'll check the hardware cost and for the growers, plain and simple, their deliveries, their pack out, their statements and not much else.
Not much else, if it's complicated they'll phone us to ask how it works which defeats the whole point.
When the truck leaves, does the driver still need a paper ticket?
Yes, the driver must leave with something in his hand, otherwise the grower phones to ask if the fruit arrived. A small printed
slip is fine, like a till slip. So a small printer next to the tablet that prints a slip for each grower on the truck. Yours. And the SMS too if they want it. But the slip
always.

And if the tablet itself rakes on a busy morning,

through the Weybridge in a day. Peak 60-70
trucks, mostly between 6 and 10 in the morning because they pick in the no, actually that's not right. They pick in the morning

growers around Enka and Kawa share transport. There's a contractor, mister Shirinza, with two trucks and he collects from six or seven growers in one trip. Right. clerk does it with a calculator. So one truck can carry several growers' bins and the weight gets shared out. Is it always by the number of bins? By
bins, we can't weigh
each bin separately, there's no bins scale. So it's the full truck minus the empty truck divided by the bins, and each grower gets his share.
and the growers accept that.

So how many bins in a day at the peak? about eighteen hundred bins a day at the peak.

phones Johan.

four hundred

and when everybody opens their statement on the same morning.

clerks at the Weybridge, one in the morning shift,

totals and the delivery numbers next to them so I can check against the tickets if a grower complains.
